Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I am permanently an outsider now
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Lukas had been deployed with a British-led unit when the incident happened, and what still returned to him most sharply was not a single clean image but the broken sequence around it: the helicopter chop overhead, a convoy halt, and the sudden sight of a man on the roadside with his leg split open and blood soaking through his trousers. He had seen injuries before, but that day the sound of aircraft above the dust, the sight of exposed wounds, and the feeling of being trapped while riding with others in a vehicle all seemed to fuse into one unbearable moment. Whenever a helicopter cut across the sky, or a stranger's cut hand or bruised face caught his eye, Lukas would be thrown straight back into that roadside scene, and the old feeling of being trapped would immediately push him into avoiding the situation altogether - changing plans, stepping away, or finding some way not to stay in it. Ever since, he found that he could be standing in his apartment in Brooklyn or at his desk drafting content calendars for his social media clients and, without warning, feel the full force of that day rush back through him with no clear picture attached to it, just a wave of dread and nausea that made him feel as if it were happening again. Other times the memory came in disconnected pieces - the smell of hot metal, a shout, the flash of red - and because it seemed so extreme, Lukas often had the unsettling sense that it could not possibly have happened to him, that it was too unreal, too severe to belong to his life. After those fragments surfaced, he would keep himself busy and keep his distance from anything that might stir them up again, telling himself that if he stayed occupied enough or left before anything escalated, he could prevent the memory from taking hold. But the more he arranged his days around avoiding those reminders, the more the memory seemed to stay vivid and close, waiting beneath the surface. That strangeness fed his conviction that he had been changed in some permanent way, and with it came the thought that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that he had failed some basic test of steadiness when others would have held it together. Once Lukas had come to see himself as permanently altered and somehow less steady than other people, ordinary cues around him took on a harsher meaning - a helicopter overhead, a uniform on the street, a glimpse of blood on a screen - all seemed to confirm the same bleak conclusion and made him more likely to pull back before they could unsettle him further.

In the months that followed, Lukas started arranging his life around what might set him off. If he saw visible injuries on someone - a scraped cyclist on the sidewalk, a cut hand in a restaurant, a swollen bruise on his girlfriend's arm after bumping into a table - he felt his chest lock and immediately began mentally rehearsing what he might say before he had to speak, especially if an interaction was expected. Those scenes carried him straight back to the roadside wound in Afghanistan, and the moment the memory hit, he would back away, look for an exit, or find a reason to leave early rather than stay and let the feeling build. He avoided military and police uniforms in public, and even a glimpse of a weapon in a film or news clip could make him pull away. Being caught in a moving car with other people brought the same response, because it revived the memory of the convoy and the sense that he had nowhere to go; when that threat felt close, he started planning routes, rides, and exits with the aim of making the world smaller and more manageable. Driving with other people became difficult because the passenger seat felt too close to being trapped again; he preferred to be alone in the car, if he drove at all. At work, where he often had to move quickly between meetings and screen calls, he became careful to avoid anything that put his body under stress - he skipped the gym, avoided running for the subway, and made excuses when colleagues suggested fast-paced team events. What frightened him most was how quickly his body reacted before he had time to reason with it: a helicopter passing over his neighborhood made his stomach drop and his hands go cold, and the old alarm could be triggered as easily by someone touching his shoulder from behind on the street. Living at that level of threat, Lukas found that almost anything could become a cue, and he responded by keeping his body in check - avoiding the gym, turning down rides, and choosing not to linger where something might catch him unprepared. Those moments of threat made him more vigilant at night, lying awake because he needed to stay alert, as if sleep itself might let something dangerous creep up on him.

The more Lukas tried to manage these reactions, the more his world narrowed. He began to go over conversations in his head before answering texts, planning sentences in advance even with his girlfriend, and he noticed that this constant checking seemed to keep the event alive rather than contain it. The effort to stay controlled also left him more on edge, and when he was already tense, the same sights and sounds that had become dangerous in his mind - helicopters, injuries, uniforms, being in a car with other people - felt even harder to tolerate. That constant managing meant the memory never really settled; the more he tried to push it away by staying busy, staying alert, and staying out of situations that might set him off, the more often the fragments broke through at night or in quiet moments, returning with the same raw force. At night, after rehearsing the next day's interactions and avoiding anything physically taxing, he would still lie awake scanning for sounds outside, and in that exhausted state the fragmented memories came back more easily, usually not as a story but as emotion without image: a pulse of panic, shame, and helplessness that seemed to rise from nowhere. Afterwards he would tell himself, with renewed bitterness, that he was permanently an outsider now, someone who no longer fit in the ordinary world of people who could watch a war scene on television or walk past an ambulance without thinking. He came to believe that his avoidance had not protected him so much as made him more fragile and more different, and that he had somehow made the whole thing harder to bear by trying to control it. In turn, that sense of being damaged and apart made the triggers feel even more charged; every helicopter, every wound, every unexpected touch seemed to confirm that he was no longer the man he had been.

By the time he sought help, Lukas had been living with this tightened circle for months. He had started turning down rides with friends, crossing the street to avoid uniforms, and stepping out of meetings to steady himself after a glimpse of someone injured in a training video. His girlfriend had begun to notice how often he scanned rooms and how often he went quiet when startled. What finally brought him to treatment was that he could no longer ignore how little sleep he was getting and how frightened he felt of his own reactions - of jerking away when touched, of feeling the rush of that day return without warning, of becoming even more cut off from others. He said he was hoping to stop feeling permanently altered, but what scared him most was the possibility that the sense of being an outsider was not a passing state at all, and that this was simply who he had become.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers but does not clearly state that they lead to maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows triggers like helicopters, injuries, and touch, but does not explicitly say they evoke the traumatic memory in a causal way within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows triggers, but it does not directly connect them to negative appraisals in a causal sequence within the same paragraph.
The vignette presents negative appraisals, but it does not explicitly state that these appraisals generate or intensify triggers within the same paragraph.
The vignette includes traumatic memory, but it does not clearly show the memory causing maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows threat and vigilance, but it does not explicitly state that threat leads to maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
The vignette includes threat, but it does not clearly state that threat itself leads to triggers within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows maladaptive strategies, but it does not explicitly state that these strategies bring back or sustain the memory within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows triggers but does not clearly state that they lead to maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows triggers like helicopters, injuries, and touch, but does not explicitly say they evoke the traumatic memory in a causal way within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers, but it does not directly connect them to negative appraisals in a causal sequence within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette presents negative appraisals, but it does not explicitly state that these appraisals generate or intensify triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette includes traumatic memory, but it does not clearly show the memory causing maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows threat and vigilance, but it does not explicitly state that threat leads to maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette includes threat, but it does not clearly state that threat itself leads to triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette shows maladaptive strategies, but it does not explicitly state that these strategies bring back or sustain the memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
